title: The US-Iran Deal Is Done. Oil Has Dropped 4 Per Cent. Here Is What It Means for India.
excerpt: The Strait of Hormuz will reopen immediately. The naval blockade is over. A signing ceremony is set for Friday in Switzerland. And India's oil import bill just got significantly lighter.
body:
The war between the United States and Iran is over — at least on paper. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced late on Sunday that Washington and Tehran have reached a deal to end hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and lift the American naval blockade that has choked global oil flows for more than three months.

"Both sides have declared the immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon," Sharif wrote on X, confirming that an official signing ceremony would take place on Friday, June 20, in Switzerland.

Minutes later, Donald Trump posted his own confirmation on Truth Social. "The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete," he wrote. "I hereby fully authorize the toll free opening of the Strait of Hormuz, and, simultaneously herewith, authorize the immediate removal of the United States Naval blockade. Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!"

## Oil Falls Sharply. India Stands to Gain the Most

Global oil prices tumbled the moment the deal broke. Brent crude fell $3.51, or 4 per cent, to $83.82. West Texas Intermediate dropped even further — down $3.93, or 4.6 per cent, to $80.95. For India, the world's third-largest oil importer, every dollar off the barrel translates into billions of rupees saved on the import bill.

The Hormuz blockade had pushed Brent above $90 for weeks, widened the current account deficit, weakened the rupee, and forced the Reserve Bank of India to burn through foreign exchange reserves at an uncomfortable pace. The reopening of the strait — which carried roughly a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the conflict — could reverse that pressure almost immediately.

Indian benchmark indices had already posted their best day in two months on Friday, with the Sensex surging nearly 1,700 points on early signs that a deal was imminent. Futures markets are signalling another strong open on Monday.

## What the Deal Includes

A senior Iranian official told Reuters that the final draft memorandum of understanding covers a sweeping set of issues. Under the agreement, Iran will immediately reopen the Strait of Hormuz to all commercial vessels, while the United States will lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports. Washington has agreed to waive oil sanctions on Iran for a specified period, release $25 billion of frozen Iranian assets through a combination of direct cash transfers and regional financial credit lines, and impose no new sanctions until a final deal is reached.

In exchange, Tehran has committed to neither producing nor acquiring nuclear weapons, maintaining the nuclear status quo — including no uranium enrichment and no expansion of nuclear facilities — and diluting its stockpile of highly enriched uranium inside Iran. A mechanism for that dilution will be discussed over 60 days of additional talks.

The New York Times reported that the biggest unresolved issue — the long-term future of Iran's nuclear programme — has been pushed to the next round of negotiations.

## The Sailors Delhi Cannot Forget

The deal arrives against the backdrop of deep Indian anger over the deaths of three Indian sailors aboard the Palau-flagged tanker Settebello, struck by U.S. precision munitions off Oman earlier this week. India summoned the American chargé d'affaires twice — a rare diplomatic escalation — and the foreign ministry called the use of "lethal and deadly force against civilian shipping" unacceptable.

The dead sailors' families, many from small towns in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, have demanded that Delhi go beyond diplomatic protests. "If he had told us about the dangers, I would have called him back," Sushila Devi, widow of one of the killed crew, told reporters in Deoria.

For India's 240,000-strong merchant marine community — many of whom have been stranded or re-routed because of the blockade — the reopening of Hormuz is not an abstraction. It is the difference between a livelihood and a death trap.

## What Comes Next

The signing ceremony on Friday in Switzerland will formalize what is, for now, a memorandum of understanding. Sixty days of technical talks will follow, covering nuclear verification, sanctions sequencing, and the future of Iranian oil on global markets.

For the Indian diaspora, the economic relief will be the first thing to land. Cheaper oil means cheaper petrol, a stronger rupee, and a narrowing current account deficit. Indian refiners — who had been scrambling for alternative crude sources — will have their pipelines restored. And NRIs watching the rupee slide all year may finally see some stabilization.

But the deeper question — whether this deal holds, or unravels the way the 2015 JCPOA did — will take months to answer. Israel, which carried out an airstrike on Beirut's southern suburbs just hours before the deal was announced, has said it is not party to the agreement. Trump himself admonished Netanyahu in a phone call, telling him, according to multiple reports, "What the f*** are you doing?"

The ceasefire is real. The oil is flowing. Whether the peace lasts is another matter entirely.
